domains.name: IL-11 Zero Trust & Endpoint Defense
domains.summary: Zero-trust architecture and endpoint defense: never trust, always verify — identity-centric access, microsegmentation, continuous verification, and endpoint detection and response, following the principles of NIST SP 800-207. This is an independent study course; it confers no certificate and claims no affiliation with any institution.

scenarios.title: The VPN is not a moat
scenarios.situation: A company routes all remote access through a VPN and treats everything inside the corporate network as trusted. An attacker phishes one employee's VPN credentials and moves laterally for six weeks undetected.
scenarios.prompt: Which zero-trust principle was violated, and what replaces the VPN-centric model?
evidence: NIST SP 800-207

NIST's Zero Trust Architecture publication defines the core tenet: never trust, always verify. Access decisions are made per-session based on identity, device posture, and context — not on network location. 'Inside the network' is not a security property.
choices: Implicit trust by network location: the fix is identity- and context-based per-request authorization (a policy decision point evaluating user, device health, and resource sensitivity every session) instead of a one-time VPN gate with a trusted interior.
The principle of least privilege was violated; the fix is a bigger VPN with more bandwidth.
No principle was violated; VPNs are zero-trust by definition.
The violated principle is defense in depth; the fix is a second VPN inside the first.
scenarios.why: A VPN moves the perimeter; zero trust removes it. Every request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted based on who and what is asking right now — location contributes context, never trust.
scenarios.hint: If the attacker is already 'inside,' what should still stop them?

scenarios.title: The alert that cried wolf
scenarios.situation: An EDR console fires 400 'suspicious PowerShell' alerts per day. Analysts have started bulk-closing them without review. Last week a real ransomware precursor hid in the noise for three days.
choices: Tune detection to the environment: baseline normal PowerShell use, write allowlisted rules for admin tooling, escalate only anomalous command lines (encoded commands, obfuscated scripts, unusual parents) — alert fidelity beats alert volume, and bulk-closing is the failure to fix.
Disable the PowerShell rule entirely; PowerShell alerts are always false positives.
Hire more analysts to close the 400 alerts by hand each day.
Uninstall PowerShell from all endpoints to eliminate the alert source.
scenarios.why: Alert fatigue is a detection-engineering failure: every unactionable alert trains analysts to ignore the actionable ones. Zero trust assumes breach — which only works if the sensors that detect breach are trustworthy.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem too many attacks, or too little tuning?

scenarios.title: Flatland
scenarios.situation: A network scan shows 2,000 hosts on a single flat /16 with no internal segmentation. Server, workstation, printer, and IoT camera traffic all mix freely; any compromised host can reach any other on any port.
scenarios.prompt: What is the misconfiguration, and what is the fix?
evidence: Microsegmentation

Zero-trust architectures shrink implicit trust zones to the smallest practical scope — ideally per-workload — so a compromised host cannot move laterally. Flat networks grant every foothold the whole estate.
choices: Missing microsegmentation: the flat /16 gives every compromised host unrestricted lateral reach — segment by workload sensitivity (servers, workstations, IoT/printers isolated with default-deny between zones) so a foothold stays a foothold.
The subnet is too large; renumbering to a /24 will fix lateral movement.
Printers need static IPs; DHCP is the vulnerability.
There is no misconfiguration; flat networks are recommended for performance.
scenarios.why: Segmentation is blast-radius engineering: assume breach, then make sure the breach cannot walk. Default-deny between zones turns one compromised camera into an incident instead of an enterprise-wide event.
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker's second step require that you can deny?

scenarios.title: Whose laptop is that?
scenarios.situation: A contractor's personal laptop — no disk encryption, OS two years out of date — authenticates with valid credentials and receives full access to the customer database because the access policy checks only username and password.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing from the access decision?
evidence: Device posture

Zero trust evaluates the subject AND the device: managed status, encryption, patch level, EDR health. Credentials prove who claims to be asking; posture proves what is asking — an untrusted device with valid credentials is still untrusted.
choices: Device trust evaluation: the policy must check device posture (managed, encrypted, patched, EDR-healthy) alongside identity — valid credentials on an unmanaged, unpatched device should get limited or no access to sensitive data.
Nothing is missing; valid credentials are sufficient for full access.
The contractor needs a stronger password; device state is irrelevant.
The database should be moved to the contractor's laptop for convenience.
scenarios.why: Identity answers 'who'; posture answers 'on what.' A policy that asks only the first question grants the keys to whoever holds the password, on whatever device they happen to own.
scenarios.hint: The credentials are valid — so what else must be true before access is granted?

scenarios.title: The service account that never sleeps
scenarios.situation: An audit finds a CI/CD service account with standing Domain Admin rights, a password unchanged in four years, used by twelve pipelines — three of which were decommissioned. The team says 'it works, don't touch it.'
scenarios.prompt: Apply least privilege and assume breach: what is the remediation plan?
choices: Eliminate standing privilege: inventory which pipelines actually need the account, scope each to just-in-time, time-bound, least-privilege credentials (short-lived tokens per pipeline), rotate or vault the secret, and remove the dead pipelines' access — 'it works' is not a security posture.
Change the password once and leave everything else as-is; rotation alone satisfies least privilege.
Grant the account Enterprise Admin so pipelines never hit permission errors.
Delete the CI/CD system; pipelines are inherently insecure.
scenarios.why: Standing privilege is pre-authorized breach: every always-on admin credential is an attacker asset waiting to be stolen. Just-in-time, scoped, expiring access gives pipelines what they need for minutes, not forever.
scenarios.hint: What does each pipeline need, for how long, and why does it still have it?

scenarios.title: Build or buy the policy engine?
scenarios.situation: A mid-size firm must choose: build a custom policy decision point (PDP) in-house, or buy a zero-trust network access (ZTNA) platform. Build costs 2 engineer-years and full maintenance liability; buy costs $180k/year with vendor lock-in and a 6-month migration.
choices: Decide on differentiation and risk: access policy enforcement is undifferentiated heavy lifting with high breach cost if wrong — buy the platform (faster, maintained, audited) unless access control is genuinely a core competency; then run a pilot measuring policy-change latency, incident response integration, and exit cost before committing.
Always build; vendor products are never trustworthy.
Always buy the cheapest option; price is the only criterion.
Defer the decision for two years; the VPN is fine until then.
scenarios.why: The trade is build-risk (you own every bug in your PDP, and auth bugs are breach bugs) versus buy-risk (lock-in, price, fit). For security infrastructure, 'boring and maintained' usually beats 'clever and yours' — measure the pilot, price the exit.
scenarios.hint: Which risk is cheaper to be wrong about: your own auth code, or a vendor contract?

domains.name: Zero Trust Architecture
domains.summary: Designing networks that never grant implicit trust: the NIST SP 800-207 tenets, identity-centric access, microsegmentation, software-defined perimeters, and continuous verification. Architecture-level thinking for containing breaches that perimeter defenses miss. This material confers no certificate and implies no vendor endorsement.

scenarios.title: The Core Idea
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks for a one-sentence definition of zero trust to anchor a new security program. Four candidate statements are on the table.
scenarios.prompt: Which statement captures zero trust correctly?
choices: Never trust, always verify — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and continuously validated regardless of network location
A strong firewall perimeter keeps everything inside it safe
All devices on the corporate LAN are trusted by default
Connecting through the VPN makes a device trusted
scenarios.why: Zero trust eliminates the idea of a trusted network: location on the LAN or VPN no longer implies trustworthiness. Every request — user, device, workload — must prove itself each time, because breaches routinely start inside the perimeter. The other options all restate the perimeter model that zero trust replaces.
scenarios.hint: What happened to the idea of a 'trusted' internal network?

scenarios.title: Identity Is the Perimeter
scenarios.situation: The company is now mostly remote. The old model — VPN into the office network, then broad internal access — has produced two incidents from compromised home machines this year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right first control to deploy?
evidence: Incident notes
Incident 1: compromised home PC -> VPN -> lateral movement to file shares.
Incident 2: stolen VPN credentials used from unknown device.
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA plus device posture checks, enforced per application session before any resource access
Longer, more complex VPN passwords
A larger, faster perimeter firewall
A policy trusting employee home Wi-Fi networks
scenarios.why: When the network cannot be trusted, identity and device health become the boundary. MFA (preferably phishing-resistant) proves who is asking; posture checks prove the device is healthy; per-session enforcement means trust is re-evaluated continuously. Longer VPN passwords do nothing against a compromised endpoint or stolen session.
scenarios.hint: If the network can't be trusted, what becomes the boundary?

scenarios.title: After the Breach
scenarios.situation: Ransomware entered through one phishing workstation and reached 400 hosts in hours. The post-incident review finds a flat /16 network: any host can talk to any host on any port.
scenarios.prompt: Which architectural change best contains the next incident?
evidence: Network diagram
Single flat VLAN: 10.0.0.0/16 — workstations, servers, printers, OT adjacent. No east-west filtering.
choices: Microsegmentation — enforce least-privilege east-west policy between workloads so a compromise cannot move laterally
Buy more antivirus licenses for the endpoints
Segment only the guest Wi-Fi — the servers are the priority
Air-gap everything and end remote work
scenarios.why: Flat networks let attackers move laterally at will — the blast radius becomes the whole enterprise. Microsegmentation carves the network into small trust zones with explicit allow-rules between them, so one compromised workstation cannot reach the server tier. It directly addresses the observed failure mode: uncontrolled east-west movement.
scenarios.hint: The attacker moved sideways — what controls sideways movement?

scenarios.title: Beyond the VPN
scenarios.situation: A third-party vendor needs access to exactly one internal application for a two-week project. The traditional answer is a full VPN tunnel into the corporate network.
scenarios.prompt: Which access model fits zero trust best?
choices: Software-defined perimeter / zero-trust network access: brokered, per-application, per-session access with no network-level trust granted
A full VPN tunnel — it is how vendor access has always been done
Publish the application's port directly to the internet
Email the vendor the data they need instead
scenarios.why: A VPN grants network-level access — far more than 'one application' — and makes the vendor's potentially unmanaged device an insider. SDP/ZTNA brokers access to the specific resource only, after verifying identity and device, with no implicit trust in the underlying network. Least privilege applied to connectivity itself.
scenarios.hint: What's the least access that still gets the job done — a network, or an application?

scenarios.title: Trust, but Continuously Verify
scenarios.situation: A user authenticated normally from headquarters at 9:00 AM. At 9:20, a login for the same account arrives from another continent on an unknown device, and immediately attempts the admin panel.
evidence: Auth events
09:00 MFA success — known device, HQ office
09:20 password-only success — unknown device, foreign ASN
09:21 admin panel access attempt
choices: Step-up authentication and session re-evaluation — continuous verification challenges or revokes the session when risk signals appear mid-session
Do nothing — the session is valid for 8 hours once authenticated
Permanently block the user — no investigation needed
Only authenticate at login — that is the industry standard
scenarios.why: Zero trust treats authentication as a moment and authorization as continuous: the policy engine re-evaluates trust as context changes. Impossible travel plus a new device plus privilege escalation is exactly the signal set that should trigger step-up auth or session termination. Login-time-only checks leave an eight-hour window for the attacker.
scenarios.hint: Authentication is a moment — what should authorization be?

scenarios.title: The Policy Engine Decision
scenarios.situation: You are designing access policy for the finance application. Options range from a static IP allowlist to a fully dynamic model, and the team worries about complexity.
scenarios.prompt: Which model aligns with zero trust, and why is the complexity worth it?
choices: Attribute-based dynamic policy — user identity, device posture, location, and risk score evaluated per session by the policy engine; it adapts to real-time risk instead of freezing yesterday's assumptions
A static IP allowlist — simple to understand and audit
Identical access for everyone — fairness and simplicity
Annual access reviews only — least administrative overhead
scenarios.why: NIST SP 800-207's tenets require access determined by dynamic policy: the observable state of the identity, the device, and behavioral attributes, evaluated per session. Static rules cannot react to compromised credentials or devices — they encode trust decisions that go stale. The complexity is the point: it is what makes access decisions reflect current reality.
scenarios.hint: NIST says access is determined by dynamic policy — what does 'dynamic' have to buy you?

lessons.title: IL-11 Zero Trust & Endpoint Defense — Core concepts
concepts: Never trust, always verify (NIST SP 800-207): every access request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted based on identity, device posture, and context — per session, per resource. Network location ('inside the VPN') is context, never a grant of trust.

Identity is the perimeter: users, workloads, and devices each get strong, phishing-resistant identity, and access policies evaluate all three. Credentials answer 'who claims to be asking'; the policy must also ask 'on what device, in what state.'

Microsegmentation shrinks implicit trust zones to the smallest practical scope — ideally per workload — with default-deny between zones. It is blast-radius engineering: assume breach, then make sure the breach cannot walk laterally.

Endpoints are the battlefield: EDR/EPP provides the detection and response sensors that 'assume breach' depends on. Alert fidelity beats alert volume — untuned detections train analysts to bulk-close, which is how real precursors hide in noise.

Least privilege is temporal as well as scoped: standing admin rights (especially service accounts) are pre-authorized breach material. Prefer just-in-time, short-lived, narrowly-scoped credentials issued per task and revoked after.

Continuous verification replaces point-in-time checks: posture, behavior, and risk are re-evaluated through the session, and access adapts or revokes as signals change. Zero trust is a control loop, not a gate — which is why it is cybernetics applied to security.

example.code:
grep -Ei 'allow.*any.*any|permit.*0\.0\.0\.0' firewall.rules | head -20
# Any hit is a candidate over-broad rule: document it,
# then check whether a narrower source/destination/port tuple suffices.
example.walkthrough: Hunting 'allow any-any' rules is the fastest zero-trust audit: each hit is implicit trust granted to the whole network. The fix pattern is always the same — replace the broad rule with the narrowest tuple the workload actually needs.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating the VPN as zero trust — a VPN moves the perimeter to the user's device; it does not verify per-request, per-resource, or continuously.
Common trap: buying EDR and skipping tuning — default detections in your environment are noise generators; fidelity comes from baselining and allowlisting your own admin tooling.
Common trap: segmenting by VLAN tag alone without policy — network separation without default-deny enforcement between zones is decoration, not microsegmentation.
Common trap: granting service accounts standing privilege 'because CI/CD needs it' — pipelines need scoped, short-lived credentials per job, not eternal Domain Admin.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Zero Trust Architecture — Core concepts
concepts: Zero trust removes implicit trust from the network: no user, device, or workload is trusted based on location — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted, per session.

NIST SP 800-207 frames this in tenets: all data sources are resources, all communication is secured regardless of location, access is granted per session by dynamic policy, and the enterprise continuously monitors asset integrity and posture.

The logical architecture has three parts: the policy engine (decides), the policy administrator (configures the decision into action), and the policy enforcement point (gates each resource) — identity and device signals feed the decision.
Microsegmentation contains lateral movement by enforcing least-privilege rules between workloads; software-defined perimeters hide resources entirely until access is brokered.
Zero trust is a program, not a product: any vendor selling 'zero trust in a box' is selling marketing. It is an ongoing architecture of identity, segmentation, and continuous verification.

example.code:
policy:
  resource: finance-app
  allow:
    - user.group: finance
      device.posture: compliant
      auth: phishing-resistant-mfa
  deny: default
example.walkthrough: A zero-trust policy states who (finance group), from what (compliant device), with how strong an authentication, may reach a resource — evaluated every session, default deny. Compare this to a firewall rule that only checks source IP: the policy engine sees identity and posture, not just packets.

pitfalls: Common trap: buying a 'zero trust' product and declaring victory — it is an architecture and operating model, not a SKU.
Common trap: equating VPN with zero trust — a VPN extends the trusted network; zero trust eliminates the concept.
Common trap: segmenting only north-south (perimeter) while leaving east-west flat — attackers live in east-west.
Common trap: authenticating once at login and never re-evaluating — sessions must reflect changing risk.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Audit for implicit trust
labs.objective: Hunt over-broad access rules in a sample firewall/policy export and rewrite the worst offenders as least-privilege tuples.
steps: Create a sample firewall.rules file with 15 rules, including 3 deliberately over-broad ones (any-any allows, wide source ranges on sensitive ports).
Run the lesson's grep to surface candidate over-broad rules.
For each hit, document the workload it supposedly serves and write the narrowest replacement rule (specific source, destination, port).
Verify no any-any rule remains and that every replacement still permits the documented workload.
Write a one-paragraph 'implicit trust inventory' summarizing what the flat rules had granted an attacker.

checks.hint: Run grep against your firewall.rules file and confirm the over-broad rules are surfaced.

labs.title: Write a conditional-access policy
labs.objective: Draft a conditional-access policy that grants database access only to healthy managed devices with phishing-resistant auth.
steps: Define three signals: user identity (MFA method strength), device posture (managed, encrypted, patched, EDR healthy), and resource sensitivity.
Write the policy as structured YAML: allow/deny/step-up rules combining the signals (e.g., unmanaged device + sensitive resource = deny).
Add a break-glass exception path with mandatory alerting and time-bounded approval.
Walk through four scenarios (managed+healthy, unmanaged, unpatched, break-glass) and record each decision.
Validate the YAML parses with python3 -c 'import yaml,json' or a JSON equivalent, and print the decision table.

checks.hint: Print your policy decision table so the word 'deny' appears in the output.

labs.title: Find the Implicit Trust
labs.objective: Audit a sample network diagram and catalog every place implicit trust is granted.
steps: Review the provided flat-network diagram and list each trust boundary (or absence of one).
Mark every spot where access is granted by network location alone.
Identify which resources would be reachable after one workstation compromise.
Propose three microsegmentation boundaries with business justification.
Rank your proposals by risk reduction per implementation effort.

checks.hint: Review your audit notes file and confirm each implicit-trust finding is documented.

labs.title: Segment a Three-Tier App
labs.objective: Draft a microsegmentation policy for a web / app / database three-tier application.
steps: Define the three tiers and the only traffic each tier legitimately needs.
Write explicit allow rules: web tier may talk to app tier on the app port only.
Set the default posture to deny, with logging on denied flows for tuning.
Add identity-aware exceptions for administrators (MFA + jump host).
Describe how you would validate the policy before enforcing it (monitor mode).

checks.hint: Check your policy draft includes an explicit default-deny rule.

simulations.title: Lateral movement in a flat network
simulations.brief: One phished workstation led to 30 compromised hosts in 4 hours. The network is flat — no segmentation, no internal access controls. Find the architectural failure.

steps.symptom: WS-118 phished 09:00. By 13:00: 30 hosts compromised, including two servers. No internal firewall rules, one broadcast domain, SMB open everywhere.
options: The users need more phishing training
Implicit trust architecture: once inside the perimeter, the attacker faced zero internal verification — the flat network treated every host as trusted
The antivirus failed
The firewall at the internet edge failed
evidence: network-map.txt
Single VLAN. No internal segmentation. SMB/RDP permitted host-to-host without authentication beyond domain membership.
timeline.txt
09:00 phish -> 09:40 lateral to 5 hosts -> 11:00 18 hosts -> 13:00 30 hosts. No internal control ever challenged the movement.
steps.explain: The perimeter held; the interior was undefended. Zero Trust's core insight: 'inside' is not a security property. Every lateral move should have faced an access decision — instead the attacker roamed a trusted interior.

steps.symptom: Architectural failure confirmed. What is the remediation that actually embodies 'never trust, always verify'?
options: A bigger perimeter firewall
Microsegmentation with identity-aware policy: every host-to-host flow requires authentication, authorization, and encryption — verified continuously, not once at the perimeter
More phishing training
Blocking SMB at the edge
evidence: zt-design.txt
Target: identity-based microsegments; default-deny between segments; continuous verification of device posture and user risk on every connection.
steps.explain: The fix moves the access decision from the perimeter to every connection. Microsegmentation plus identity-aware policy means the next phished workstation is an island, not a beachhead.

simulations.debrief: Flat networks convert one compromise into thirty. Zero Trust puts an access decision on every flow — verify explicitly, grant least privilege, assume breach — so lateral movement dies at the first hop.

simulations.title: The contractor and the production database
simulations.brief: A contractor needs production database access for a 3-day migration. Their laptop is unmanaged, and they are working from a hotel network. Make the access decision.

steps.symptom: Request: direct DB access, unmanaged device, untrusted network, 3-day window, production data.
options: Grant VPN access — the migration is urgent

Conditional access: managed-session via privileged access workstation or VDI, MFA with phishing-resistant factor, time-boxed just-in-time role, session recording, no direct network path from the unmanaged device to the DB
Deny outright — contractors never touch prod
Email them the credentials
evidence: risk.txt
Unmanaged device + untrusted network + prod data = maximum risk combination. Direct access would violate every Zero Trust principle simultaneously.
zt-policy.txt
Access decisions evaluate identity + device posture + network + risk, every session. Unmanaged devices get mediated sessions (VDI/PAW), never direct paths to crown jewels.
steps.explain: Zero Trust does not say 'no' — it says 'verify, then grant the minimum through the safest path.' The contractor gets the work done inside a recorded, time-boxed, mediated session; the unmanaged laptop never touches the database network.

steps.symptom: The contractor complains the VDI session is slow and asks for direct access 'just for an hour.' Your answer?
options: Grant the hour — it is only 60 minutes
Hold the line: investigate the VDI performance issue instead, and keep the mediated path — exceptions for convenience are how perimeters die
Grant direct access but watch the logs
Cancel the migration
evidence: perf.txt
VDI slowness traced to hotel Wi-Fi, not the VDI stack. Workaround: async batch jobs submitted through the session. Direct access still denied.
steps.explain: Every 'just this once' is a precedent. Fix the underlying friction (the network, the workflow) rather than the security control — convenience exceptions compound into architecture.

simulations.debrief: Zero Trust access decisions weigh all signals — identity, device, network, risk — and grant the minimum through the safest path. The policy bends for legitimate need via safer alternatives, never via exceptions.

simulations.title: EDR flags the CFO's laptop
simulations.brief: EDR: credential-dumping behavior on LAPTOP-CFO at 10:15. The CFO is in back-to-back meetings and unreachable. The device holds cached credentials for finance systems. Respond.

steps.symptom: EDR high-severity: lsass access from an unsigned binary on LAPTOP-CFO. User context: cfo. Device compliance: healthy, 2 hours ago.
options: Wait for the CFO to confirm — it might be legitimate
Assume breach: isolate the device, revoke the user's sessions and tokens, force step-up re-authentication on finance systems — then investigate
Wipe the laptop immediately
Ignore — the device was compliant
evidence: edr.txt
10:15 unsigned process read lsass memory. 10:16 outbound connection to unknown IP. No IT ticket for admin work on this device.
zt-playbook.txt
Continuous verification: a healthy attestation from 2 hours ago is stale the moment behavior contradicts it. Trust is re-evaluated on every signal.
steps.explain: Assume breach means the alert is guilty until the investigation acquits it — especially with finance-system credentials at stake. Isolation plus session revocation contains the blast radius in minutes; the CFO's meeting is not worth the domain.

steps.symptom: Device isolated, sessions revoked. Investigation: the CFO's teenager installed a 'game mod' that bundled the dumper. What completes the response?
options: Unisolate and apologize

Verify no lateral movement or data access occurred during the window, rotate the exposed credentials, re-image the device, and enforce application control so unsigned binaries cannot run on privileged devices
Ban the teenager from the laptop
Buy the CFO a new laptop
evidence: scope.txt
Window 10:15–10:22. No lateral movement detected; one finance share enumerated, no files opened. Cached credentials rotated.
steps.explain: Scope the window, rotate what was exposed, rebuild trust in the device (re-image), and close the control gap (application control on high-value endpoints). The root cause is architectural: privileged users' devices must not run unsigned code.

simulations.debrief: Continuous verification means trust expires on evidence, not on schedule. Isolate fast, revoke sessions, scope the window, rebuild the device — and make the control that would have prevented it permanent.

simulations.title: The legacy protocol bypassing MFA
simulations.brief: MFA is enforced everywhere — yet the auth logs show successful logons with no MFA challenge from a legacy inventory system. Find the bypass.

steps.symptom: 200 successful logons this month with auth method 'NTLM', zero MFA challenges, all from the legacy inventory app's service account.
options: The MFA server is misconfigured
Legacy protocol bypass: the app authenticates via NTLM, which never triggers the MFA policy — the 'MFA everywhere' claim has a protocol-shaped hole
Users are sharing MFA tokens
The logs are wrong
evidence: auth-log.txt
200 logons: protocol NTLMv2, MFA challenge: none (policy only applies to modern auth flows). Account: SVC-inventory, member of Domain Users, interactive logon rights.
mfa-policy.txt
MFA enforced on: web SSO, VPN, RDP gateway. Not covered: NTLM, legacy IMAP/SMTP auth, direct LDAP binds.
steps.explain: MFA policies are only as complete as the protocols they cover. Legacy protocols that predate modern auth silently bypass the control — the inventory app has a permanent MFA exemption nobody approved.

steps.symptom: Bypass confirmed. What is the fix that honors 'verify explicitly'?
options: Disable the inventory app
Block legacy auth at the identity provider, migrate the app to modern auth (or isolate it behind an app proxy with MFA), and audit all accounts for legacy-protocol usage
Add a second password for the service account
Monitor the NTLM logons and hope
evidence: remediation.txt
NTLM blocked tenant-wide; inventory app moved behind app proxy with pre-auth MFA; legacy-auth audit found 3 more service accounts, all remediated.
steps.explain: Verify explicitly means no protocol gets a free pass. Kill legacy auth, give the app a modern path (or a proxied one), and audit for the same hole elsewhere — bypasses travel in packs.

simulations.debrief: Audit your MFA coverage by protocol, not by policy document. Every legacy auth path is an MFA bypass until proven otherwise — find them with the logs before the attacker does.

simulations.title: Segment the three-tier app
simulations.brief: The customer portal is three tiers — web, app, DB — on one flat segment. Design the Zero Trust segmentation: which flows are allowed, and what verifies them?

steps.symptom: Current: web/app/DB all on 10.2.0.0/16, any-to-any. DB holds customer PII.
options: Put a firewall between the app and the internet

Three microsegments with explicit allow edges: internet->web (443), web->app (defined API port), app->DB (DB port, app identity only); default-deny everything else; every edge requires mutual TLS with workload identity
Move the DB to the cloud
Encrypt the database
evidence: flow-log.txt
Legitimate flows: 443 in, web->app:8443, app->db:5432. Everything else (all other observed flows): scanning, admin RDP, backup agents — each needs its own explicit edge or it dies.
zt-principles.txt
Microsegmentation + explicit allow + workload identity + encryption on every edge. The DB never sees a packet that the app tier did not cryptographically vouch for.
steps.explain: The design follows the actual traffic: allow the three legitimate edges, deny the universe, and authenticate the workloads (not just the network location) on each edge. The DB becomes reachable only through the app's identity.

steps.symptom: The backup agent needs DB access but lives outside the app segment. How does it fit the model?
options: Open the DB segment to the backup VLAN
Give the backup workload its own identity and an explicit, scheduled edge: backup-identity -> DB on the backup port, only during the backup window, logged and alerted otherwise
Run backups from the app tier
Skip backups for the DB
evidence: edge-spec.txt
Edge: backup-svc -> db:5432, window 02:00–03:00, mTLS workload identity, all other times: deny + alert.
steps.explain: Zero Trust does not forbid the backup — it gives it a named, bounded, verified edge instead of a hole in the segment. Every exception becomes an explicit edge with conditions, never a flat 'allow.'

simulations.debrief: Microsegmentation is allowlisting for network flows: explicit edges between verified workload identities, default-deny between them. Every 'exception' is just another explicit edge with conditions.

consoleSims.title: Enforce default-deny on the segment
consoleSims.brief: Allow the identity provider (10.0.5.10) to reach TCP 443 on INPUT, then set the INPUT default policy to DROP.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule accepting TCP port 443 from 10.0.5.10 on INPUT.
tasks.hint: Add an INPUT rule: protocol tcp, port 443, source 10.0.5.10, action ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user

Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)

Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?

Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
